title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compared two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run used gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; preregistration employed shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task pair received one LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Important clarifications: the preregistered hypotheses H1/H2 about comparative architecture performance under independent generation and repair were not exercised by this execution because of the deliberate shared_initial_candidate design; the measured estimand is validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates. Provider‑call and reconciliation artifacts (see Methods) corroborate execution isolation and absence of prompt contamination. Representative per‑task validator traces (scoring JSONs) show parsed_command_count = required_command_count and repair_applied = false for typical tasks, explaining why repair loops were not invoked. The archived bundle contains the full execution and analysis manifests, per‑task validator traces, and the preregistration.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, absence of transient safety violations) while supporting diverse intents across vendor CLIs. Two architectural approaches are often proposed: (A) translation‑first pipelines that restrict generation to a vendor DSL and apply formal verification and solver feedback, and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines that centralize generation in an LLM and rely on deterministic validators plus bounded repair. Prior work documents both deterministic verification strengths and LLM‑driven flexibility, but artifactized, preregistered head‑to‑head comparisons with per‑task validator traces are scarce.

This study's preregistered question was: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (measured by deterministic validation: reachability and policy isolation) — (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed a paired design (N = 120 paired tasks), the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B), the generator (gpt‑5‑mini), the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1).

A key, deliberate preregistered design choice was shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired task we generated a single LLM candidate and supplied the identical candidate to both downstream arms. This narrows the confirmatory estimand to validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates (i.e., whether downstream orchestration and verification produce different deterministic acceptance outcomes for the same textual proposal). The manuscript highlights this restriction throughout: the numerical results therefore answer the restricted (but operationally meaningful) validator‑parity question, not the broader generator/repair robustness hypotheses H1 and H2, which remain preregistered but unobserved under the chosen generation semantics.
sections.related_work:
Two research traditions frame our contribution and motivate the experimental axes: (1) formal translation and verification systems that prioritize deterministic guarantees through constrained DSL synthesis and solver checks, and (2) LLM‑driven agentic NetOps that emphasize flexible generation plus iterative repair and verifier loops. Representative work on constrained synthesis and deterministic verification (e.g., SymNet, “Don’t Mind the Gap”, and recent Weighted NetKAT extensions) focuses on bounded output surfaces and formal acceptance semantics [10,11,5]. Recent LLM‑centric NetOps and AIOps studies instrument generate→validate→repair pipelines, sample generator variance, and track repair coverage and transient unsafe proposals [3,4].

Methodologically these families differ along four axes we emphasize: independent generation sampling (single vs multiple draws per arm), repair‑loop instrumentation and budget, validator‑acceptance focus (binary gate vs graded diagnostics), and emulator/hardware realism. Our preregistered design placed this run at the validator‑acceptance end of the spectrum by holding generator output fixed per pair (shared_initial_candidate), intentionally isolating downstream acceptance differences.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and execution contract. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed the primary estimand (paired difference A − B), N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks, generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, maximum_model_calls = 240, and shared_initial_candidate semantics. Analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 with bootstrap percentile CIs and an exact McNemar test. The preregistration, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived in the bundle referenced in the disclosure.

Task generation and canonical references. Confirmatory tasks (120 pairs) were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each manifest entry (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) includes the intent text, canonical reference answer, initial and expected final states, required safe sequences, and difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, difficulty level). Representative manifest entries and their canonical reference answers are archived and serve as the validator's normalization targets.

Shared‑candidate orchestration and provider audit. Orchestration implemented shared_initial_candidate: for each pair the system made one LLM call and distributed the identical textual candidate to both arms. Execution accounting (execution/execution_manifest.json) records planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, and model_calls_used = 120. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) report hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, and no provider failures—these provider‑audit fields corroborate execution isolation and that a single, fresh generation was used per pair.

Provider‑call traces and contamination checks (required revision). Provider‑call traces are archived and contain the model invocation record fields (for example: system_prompt, user_prompt, model_response, metadata). Representative traces (execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json, execution/provider_calls/task-000002-shared-initial.json, execution/provider_calls/task-000003-shared-initial.json) show the user_prompt field equal to the task.intent and generation constraints from the task manifest; they do not include the canonical reference_answer field from the manifest. The analysis/contamination_summary.csv and deterministic_reconciliation.json contain the preregistered contamination diagnostic outputs; no contamination flags were produced. These artifacts together demonstrate that canonical reference answers were not injected into per‑task LLM user prompts and that prompt/response contamination across paired runs was not observed under the recorded provider audit fields.

Deterministic validator and scoring. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applies full_intent_constraint_validation: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion, ordering/dependency checks (make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore), final state consistency checks, and emits validation_after.valid (boolean). A configuration is scored success (1) only when validation_after.valid == true. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record normalized_response, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, and repair_applied flags; these per‑task JSONs are the canonical, archived evidence for each decision.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The execution manifest records planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 120 (one shared LLM call per pair), and maximum_model_calls = 240. Deterministic reconciliation confirms complete_pair_count = 120 and provider audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 120, cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false.

Contingency and statistical summaries. The analysis contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Marginal success rates are baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 and guarded = 120/120 = 1.0; observed paired difference A − B = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) returned [0.00,0.00]. Exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. These statistics are deterministic given the degenerate contingency table.

Why repairs were never invoked (required revision). Per‑task scoring JSONs archive the mechanistic fields that explain the absence of repairs. Representative examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json shows parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4 and repair_applied = false; execution/scoring/task-000002-baseline.json shows parsed_command_count = 2, required_command_count = 2 and repair_applied = false; execution/scoring/task-000003-baseline.json shows parsed_command_count = 6, required_command_count = 6 and repair_applied = false. The identical guarded traces (execution/scoring/task-00000X-guarded.json) record the same counts and repair_applied = false. These archived equality fields (parsed_command_count == required_command_count) are the concrete evidence that the shared LLM candidates satisfied the validator's required commands and ordering checks and therefore did not trigger the repair subsystem. Aggregation across all episodes shows repair_applied count = 0; this absence is recorded in analysis/condition_summary.csv and the scoring JSONs.

Contamination and missingness diagnostics. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty (no flags), and analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 with zero failed or unscorable episodes. Provider audit and reconciliation artifacts (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) show no retries beyond the preregistered policy and no cross‑condition cache reuse; together these artifacts corroborate the claim that execution isolation and contamination checks passed.
sections.discussion:
What the run measures — and what it does not. By design the shared_initial_candidate semantics remove generator variance from the confirmatory estimand: the run answers whether downstream orchestration and verification produce different deterministic acceptance outcomes for identical textual proposals (validator‑acceptance parity). The observed complete concordance (n11 = 120) directly answers this restricted question: both pipeline arms accepted the identical candidates for every paired task under deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The run does not exercise independent generator sampling, multi‑sample selection, or repair efficacy; consequently the preregistered H1/H2 about generator/repair performance are preregistered but unobserved under this execution.

Artifact‑grounded mechanistic interpretation. The provider_call traces (e.g., execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json) document that per‑task user_prompt fields contained only the task intent and generation constraints (no canonical reference answer), while the scoring JSONs record parsed_command_count == required_command_count and repair_applied = false for typical tasks (examples cited in Results). These archived facts explain why repairs were not invoked and demonstrate that validator acceptance was driven by candidate content satisfying required sequence and ordering constraints rather than by prompt leakage.

Design consequences and actionable follow‑ups. To test the original H1/H2 claims about independent generation and repair performance, the preregistered protocol must be altered to (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives an independent LLM generation per pair (this doubles initial model_calls_used from 120 to 240), (ii) enable independent sampling or multiple initial candidates per arm to estimate generator variance, and (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations so repair_applied > 0 becomes observable. Each modification would leave distinct, archived signatures (increased hosted_model_call_event_count, nonzero repair_provider_trace paths in execution/scoring/*.json) making follow‑up confirmatory tests artifact‑traceable. The preregistration documents these resource and instrumentation tradeoffs and the exact artifacts that would change under such a follow‑up.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared_candidate design intentionally removed generator variance and thus strengthens internal identifiability for the validator‑parity estimand; it is a deliberate restriction, not an execution failure. Construct validity: binary validator acceptance is operationally conservative and omits maintainability, explanation, and human‑operator trust dimensions; per‑task parsed and violation fields are archived and enable richer construct checks if desired. External validity: the synthetic Mininet‑derived corpus, a single model (gpt‑5‑mini), and a single deterministic validator limit generality. Conclusion validity: the degenerate contingency produces a point mass CI and p = 1.0; the analysis artifacts document the exact seeds and bootstrap parameters so alternate designs can be power‑analyzed reproducibly.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifactized paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair NetOps pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks deterministic validators accepted identical LLM candidates in both arms for every pair (n11 = 120), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); thus preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage are unobserved in this execution. The run precisely measures validator‑acceptance parity under controlled shared candidates and provides an artifact bundle and explicit, artifact‑referenced protocol modifications for future discriminating comparisons that exercise independent generation and repair coverage.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
